analogy.p: A thermostat has a sensor (receptor) that detects room temperature, a control unit (coordination centre) that compares it with the set temperature, and a boiler or radiator (effector) that switches on when it is too cold and off when it is warm enough. This keeps the temperature close to the setting just as negative feedback keeps the body near its optimum. It breaks down because a thermostat only controls heating, while the body has opposite effectors (sweating and shivering) to push in both directions, and the body's set points are controlled by living tissue, not a dial.

bullets: Learn the definition word for word: regulation of internal conditions, to maintain optimum conditions, in response to internal and external changes.
It is **automatic**: you do not consciously decide to sweat or to release insulin.
It maintains conditions at or near an **optimum**, not at one exact fixed value; values fluctuate slightly around it.
It operates in cells (for example regulating water content) and in whole organisms.
In the human body it includes control of **blood glucose concentration**, **body temperature** and **water levels**.
Homeostasis is a feature of mammals and many other organisms, helping them live in a wide range of environments.
core.p: **Homeostasis** is the **regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes**. Your surroundings and your own activities constantly push your internal conditions up and down, for example when you exercise, eat or step into cold air. Homeostasis uses automatic control systems to cancel out those changes and keep conditions in a narrow range. The word 'internal' matters: homeostasis controls conditions inside the body, not the outside world.

bullets: Enzymes have an **optimum temperature**; for human enzymes this is about **37 degrees C** (body temperature).
Above the optimum the enzyme's **active site** changes shape and the substrate no longer fits: the enzyme is **denatured** (permanent).
Below the optimum there is less kinetic energy, fewer successful collisions and a **lower rate** of reaction.
Enzymes also have an optimum **pH**; this is why chemical conditions must be stable too.
Too little glucose in the blood means cells cannot respire enough to release energy; too much can damage tissue and draws water out of cells by osmosis.
If the water content of body fluids changes, cells can **swell or shrink** because of osmosis.
Therefore failure of homeostasis leads to **disease** or even death.
core.p: Homeostasis **maintains optimal conditions for enzyme action and all cell functions**. Enzymes are biological catalysts with a particular shape, and their activity depends on temperature and pH. If the temperature rises too far, the enzyme's active site changes shape and the enzyme is **denatured**; if it falls too low, molecules move more slowly and reactions are too slow. Cells also need a steady supply of glucose for respiration and a correct water balance so they do not gain or lose too much water by osmosis.

bullets: **Blood glucose concentration**: controlled by hormones insulin and glucagon released by the **pancreas**.
**Body temperature**: kept at about **37 degrees C**, using the skin, the brain and effectors such as sweat glands and muscles.
**Water levels**: controlled by the brain, the pituitary gland, hormone ADH and the kidneys (triple detail).
Blood glucose and water control use **hormones** (chemical responses); temperature control uses nervous responses plus other mechanisms.
All three keep the conditions inside cells and tissue fluid suitable for **enzyme action**.
Other variables controlled by the body include pH and carbon dioxide concentration, but these are not the named examples.
core.h: The three conditions you must know
core.p: The specification names three examples of conditions controlled by homeostasis in the human body: **blood glucose concentration**, **body temperature** and **water levels**. Each is controlled by a different set of organs but all follow the same pattern of control system. In this topic you only need the general idea and the components; the details of each condition are separate spec points (blood glucose and diabetes, control of body temperature, water balance and the kidneys).

bullets: **Receptors**: cells that **detect stimuli** (changes in the environment).
**Coordination centres**: receive and process information from receptors, e.g. the **brain**, **spinal cord** and **pancreas**.
**Effectors**: **muscles or glands** that bring about responses which restore optimum levels.
**Stimulus** = a change that is detected, e.g. a rise in temperature.
**Response** = what the effector does, e.g. sweat release or shivering.
Describe the whole pathway in order; examiners give marks for each correct component in a chain.
Information travels between components as **nerve impulses** or as **hormones** in the blood.
core.p: All automatic control systems have three parts: **receptors**, **coordination centres** and **effectors**. A receptor detects a **stimulus**, which is a change in the environment. The coordination centre receives information from receptors, processes it and decides what response is needed. The effector then carries out the response, which should **restore the optimum level**. These three parts work in a chain: stimulus, receptor, coordination centre, effector, response.

bullets: A receptor detects a **specific type of stimulus**.
Examples: **temperature receptors in the skin** and brain; **light receptors** in the retina; **glucose-sensitive cells** in the pancreas.
Receptors convert the stimulus into an **electrical impulse** (nervous system) or trigger a chemical signal.
Receptors can be in sense organs or inside the body.
The pancreas acts as a receptor for blood glucose and also as a coordination centre.
Receptors are the starting point of every control system; a faulty receptor leads to a faulty response.
Receptors should not be confused with effectors: receptors **detect**, effectors **respond**.
core.p: Receptors are specialised cells (or the parts of cells) that detect specific stimuli. Different receptors are sensitive to different stimuli, for example temperature receptors, light receptors in the eye, and cells in the pancreas that detect blood glucose concentration. When the receptor detects a change it passes the information onwards to the coordination centre either as an electrical impulse in a nerve or by chemical signals. Without a receptor, the body would not know that a condition had changed, and no correction could happen.

bullets: Examples named in the spec: **brain**, **spinal cord** and **pancreas**.
The **brain and spinal cord** form the central nervous system (CNS).
The coordination centre receives **impulses** or chemical signals from receptors.
It decides the response and sends **impulses** (to muscles) or releases **hormones** (to glands, liver, kidneys).
In body temperature control the coordination centre is the thermoregulatory centre in the brain.
In reflexes, the spinal cord is the coordination centre.
The coordination centre is where information is **processed**, so it must connect to both receptors and effectors.
core.p: The coordination centre is the part of the control system that receives and processes information from receptors. In nervous responses the coordination centres are the **brain** and **spinal cord**, which together make up the **central nervous system (CNS)**. In hormonal responses organs such as the **pancreas** act as the coordination centre. The coordination centre compares the information with the optimum and chooses an appropriate response, sending a message to the effector.

bullets: Two types of effector: **muscles** (contract) and **glands** (secrete).
Muscle examples: skeletal muscles that shiver; muscles in the iris; muscles in blood vessel walls.
Gland examples: **sweat glands**, the **pancreas** (insulin and glucagon), adrenal glands.
Effector responses are intended to **restore** the optimum.
The effector response is sometimes called the **corrective response**.
Hormones travel in the blood to a **target organ** (also an effector) such as the liver.
Always name the specific effector in a context question (e.g. 'sweat glands' not just 'glands').
core.p: Effectors are the **muscles or glands** that bring about responses to restore optimum levels. A **muscle** effector responds by contracting (for example shivering muscles generate heat). A **gland** effector responds by secreting a chemical, such as sweat glands releasing sweat or the pancreas releasing insulin. Effectors are what actually change the internal condition, so they must act in the correct direction to oppose the original change.

bullets: **Nervous**: electrical **impulses** along neurones; very **fast**; effects are **short lived**; acts on a **precise** target.
**Hormonal (chemical)**: hormones travel in the **blood**; **slower**; effects **last longer**; may act on **several** target organs.
Nervous responses are used for rapid action (reflexes, shivering).
Hormonal responses are used for longer-term changes (blood glucose, growth).
The **blood** is the transport system for hormones, which is why hormone effects take longer to start.
Exam command: 'compare' needs a comparison in each point, e.g. 'nervous responses are fast whereas hormonal responses are slower'.
Hormones are made by **endocrine glands**, for example pancreas, pituitary, thyroid.
core.p: Automatic control systems may involve **nervous responses** or **chemical responses**. In a nervous response, **nerve impulses** (electrical signals) travel along neurones from receptor to coordination centre to effector. In a chemical response, a **hormone** is secreted by a gland into the blood and carried to a target organ. Many homeostatic systems, such as temperature control, use both. Knowing the differences helps you to explain why a response is fast or slow.

bullets: Negative feedback = a change is detected and the response **opposes** the change.
If the level **rises** above optimum, the response makes it **fall**.
If the level **falls** below optimum, the response makes it **rise**.
The effect is **stability**: conditions stay close to optimum.
The response stops when the optimum is restored, saving energy.
Analogy: a room thermostat switching a heater on and off.
The term appears explicitly in the specification in the control of thyroxine (triple), but the principle underlies all homeostasis.
Negative feedback is the opposite of positive feedback, where a change causes more change; positive feedback is not needed for the homeostasis examples.
core.p: Homeostatic systems work by **negative feedback**. When a condition moves away from its optimum, the control system detects the change and triggers a response that **reverses** it, bringing it back. As the level returns to normal, the response switches off. Because the system keeps correcting in both directions, the condition fluctuates in a narrow range around the set point rather than staying exactly constant.

bullets: Stimulus: body temperature rises above or falls below about **37 degrees C**.
Receptors: **thermoreceptors** in the skin and brain.
Coordination: **thermoregulatory centre** in the brain.
Effectors: **sweat glands**, **skeletal muscles**, blood vessels in the skin (vasodilation / vasoconstriction).
Response when too hot: more **sweating**, vasodilation; when too cold: **shivering**, less sweat, vasoconstriction.
Result: temperature returns to optimum, so enzymes keep working efficiently.
This detail is covered fully in the separate spec point on control of body temperature.
core.p: Body temperature is a good example to practise. The receptors are **temperature receptors in the skin** and in the brain. The **thermoregulatory centre in the brain** is the coordination centre. The effectors include **sweat glands** (to cool) and **muscles** (shivering to warm). If body temperature rises, sweating increases and heat is lost by evaporation of sweat; if it falls, shivering generates heat by respiration in muscles.

bullets: Stimulus: change in blood glucose concentration.
Receptor and coordination centre: the **pancreas**.
Effectors: **liver** and **muscle cells** (and other cells taking up glucose).
High glucose: **insulin** released, glucose enters cells and is stored as glycogen, blood glucose falls.
Low glucose: **glucagon** released, glycogen broken down to glucose, blood glucose rises.
This is a hormonal (chemical) negative feedback loop.
Failure of this system leads to **diabetes**; covered in the next spec point.
core.p: After a meal, carbohydrate is digested to glucose, which is absorbed into the blood, so blood glucose concentration rises. The **pancreas** detects this and releases the hormone **insulin** into the blood. Insulin makes glucose move out of the blood into cells and be stored in the liver and muscles as **glycogen**, so blood glucose falls back to normal. If blood glucose falls too low, the pancreas releases **glucagon**, causing glycogen to be converted back to glucose.

bullets: Water leaves the body via urine, sweat and breathing out.
Stimulus: the water content of the blood falls or rises.
The **brain** detects the change; the **pituitary gland** releases **ADH** into the blood.
Effector: the **kidneys** change the volume and concentration of urine.
Too little water: ADH increases, **less, concentrated urine**.
Too much water: ADH decreases, **more, dilute urine**.
Detailed study is in the triple-only spec point on the kidneys and water balance.
core.h: Applying the model: water levels (triple detail)
core.p: Water content of the blood must stay within narrow limits so that cells do not gain or lose too much water by osmosis. Water is lost in sweat, in breath and in **urine**. The brain monitors blood water content and, when it falls, the **pituitary gland** releases the hormone **ADH**, which makes the kidneys reabsorb more water, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. This is a negative feedback loop involving a hormone and an effector organ.

bullets: Failure of blood glucose control: **diabetes**.
Failure of temperature control: **hyperthermia** (too hot) or **hypothermia** (too cold).
Failure of water balance: **dehydration** or overhydration.
Conditions outside the narrow range can cause enzymes to **denature** or cells to be damaged.
Medical treatments (such as insulin injections) replace or support the failed part of the system.
Homeostatic failure shows why every component is essential.
Exam answers should link the failure to a particular receptor, coordination centre or effector.
core.p: If a control system breaks down or is overwhelmed, internal conditions drift away from the optimum and cells stop working properly. Disease can affect receptors, coordination centres or effectors. For example, in type 1 diabetes the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, so blood glucose is not controlled. In extreme heat the body may not lose heat fast enough, causing heat stroke, whereas prolonged exposure to cold causes hypothermia.

bullets: **Enzymes**: optimum temperature and pH are the reason homeostasis exists.
**Osmosis**: water balance prevents cells swelling or shrinking.
**Respiration**: glucose supply and heat from respiration depend on controlled conditions.
**Nervous system and reflexes**: receptors, CNS and effectors in nervous responses.
**Hormones**: insulin, glucagon, ADH, thyroxine and others carry chemical messages.
**Plants**: plants also coordinate responses, but with hormones only (tropisms).
**Required practical**: reaction time looks at the nervous system response.
core.p: Homeostasis is a theme running through the whole of AQA Biology. It links enzymes, respiration, osmosis, the nervous system and the endocrine system together. Use these links to build extended answers, such as 6-mark questions about control of body temperature or blood glucose.

bullets: Identify the **set point** first; say the level 'fluctuates around the optimum' rather than 'stays constant'.
Quote **two data points with units** (for example mmol/dm3 or degrees C) when describing a rise or fall.
A **rise above** the optimum triggers a response that makes the level **fall** (negative feedback); a fall below triggers a response that makes it **rise**.
Name the specific receptor and effector for the condition shown, not just 'the body'.
Explain **why** the correction matters: enzymes and cells only work well near the optimum.
A flat line after a disturbance shows the control system has restored the optimum; a line that never returns suggests failure (for example diabetes).
Time delays in hormonal control mean the correction is slower and may overshoot slightly before settling.
Use the command word: 'describe' = what the line does; 'explain' = which components cause it.
core.p: Exam questions often show a graph of a condition such as blood glucose concentration or body temperature against time, and ask you to describe and explain what is happening. Start by finding the **optimum (set point)** and the normal range, then describe where the line goes above or below it, quoting values and units from the axes. Then explain the correction: when the level is above the optimum the effector acts to make it fall, and when it is below the optimum the effector acts to make it rise. A line that wobbles around the set point rather than sitting on it is exactly what homeostasis produces, because it is a continuous cycle of detection and correction.

exam: **State/Name** (1 mark): give the term, e.g. 'effector'. **Define** homeostasis: use the full spec wording, 2 marks.
For 'explain why homeostasis is important' (2 to 3 marks): optimum conditions for **enzyme action** and all cell functions; enzymes denature if too hot / too slow if too cold.
For 'describe how a control system works': receptor detects stimulus, coordination centre processes, effector responds, optimum restored.
Always name specific examples: e.g. receptor = temperature receptors in skin, effector = sweat glands.
For negative feedback: say the response 'reverses / opposes the change' and 'returns the level to the optimum'.
Compare nervous and hormonal control with points of comparison: speed, duration, pathway (neurones vs blood), target.
Graph questions: identify the set point, describe fluctuations around it and explain what the effector does when above or below.
Use data: quote values from tables when asked and give units (e.g. mmol/dm3 or degrees C).
6-mark questions: structure as stimulus, receptor, coordination centre, effector, response, feedback.
Avoid vague words like 'it balances out'; use 'maintains optimum', 'restores', 'detects', 'secretes'.

mistakes.r: Homeostasis maintains conditions at or near the optimum, with small fluctuations around it.
It regulates INTERNAL conditions of the cell or organism.
Receptors detect the stimulus; effectors (muscles or glands) bring about the response.
Coordination centres include the brain, spinal cord and pancreas.
mistakes.w: The brain is the only coordination centre.

mistakes.r: Hormones are carried in the blood; nerve impulses travel along neurones.
Enzymes are not alive; they are denatured because their active site changes shape.
mistakes.w: Enzymes die when it is too hot.

mistakes.r: 'Negative' means the response reverses (opposes) the change, restoring the optimum.
mistakes.w: Negative feedback means a bad response.

mistakes.r: Nervous responses are faster; hormonal responses are slower but last longer.
mistakes.w: Hormonal responses are faster than nervous.

summary: AQA expects you to define homeostasis, explain why it maintains optimum conditions for enzyme action and cell function, name the three conditions controlled in humans (blood glucose, body temperature, water levels), and describe how every control system uses receptors, coordination centres and effectors. It matters because it is the framework for all later topics in homeostasis and response.

terms.d: The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function in response to internal and external changes.
A cell that detects a stimulus (a change in the environment).
A change in the environment that is detected by a receptor.
A region (such as the brain, spinal cord or pancreas) that receives and processes information from receptors.
A muscle or gland that brings about a response to restore optimum levels.
The action of an effector following a stimulus.
A control mechanism in which a change is detected and the response reverses it, restoring the optimum.
The condition at which a body process, such as enzyme action, works best.
A chemical messenger secreted by a gland and carried in the blood to a target organ.
A response in which electrical impulses pass along neurones from receptor to effector.
A biological catalyst, a protein that speeds up reactions without being used up.
Having an active site whose shape has changed so the enzyme can no longer bind its substrate.
The amount of glucose dissolved in the blood, controlled by insulin and glucagon.
An organ that secretes chemical substances such as hormones.
The optimum value around which a condition is held.
A receptor that detects changes in temperature, for example in the skin and brain.
A hormone from the pancreas that lowers blood glucose concentration.
Anti-diuretic hormone, released by the pituitary gland, which changes the volume and concentration of urine to control water levels.

worked.ans: Controlling temperature keeps enzymes at their optimum, so cell reactions occur at the best rate. Too high denatures enzymes; too low slows reactions.
worked.q: Explain why it is important that body temperature is controlled. (3 marks)
steps: Enzymes control the reactions in cells and have an optimum temperature (about 37 degrees C).
If temperature rises too high the active site changes shape and enzymes are denatured.
If temperature falls too low, enzyme activity slows, so reactions are too slow.

worked.ans: The pancreas detects the rise and releases insulin. The liver and muscles remove glucose from the blood, so the concentration returns to normal.
worked.q: After a meal a person's blood glucose concentration rises. Name the receptor, coordination centre and effector and describe the response. (4 marks)
steps: Receptor/coordination centre: the pancreas detects the high glucose concentration.
The pancreas secretes insulin into the blood.
Effectors: liver and muscle cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen.
Blood glucose falls back to the optimum (negative feedback).

worked.ans: Nervous responses are fast, short-lived and use impulses along neurones; hormonal responses are slower, longer lasting and use hormones carried in the blood.
worked.q: Compare nervous responses and hormonal responses in homeostasis. (4 marks)
steps: Nervous responses use electrical impulses; hormonal use chemicals in the blood.
Nervous are fast; hormonal are slower.
Nervous effects are short-lived; hormonal effects last longer.
Nervous act on a precise target; hormones can act on target organs wherever the blood carries them.
